scenario: A landlord whose tenant Pemberton moved out and left the unit a mess uploads three photos and two CSV files (an Austin housing file and a restoration-specs file). They ask the agent to list the repair, cleaning, and renovation jobs, assign each to a contractor, draft a text to each contractor including the property name, unit, and address, run a return-on-investment comparison of a premium versus standard renovation using a price-to-rent rule, update a memory file with unit status, total portfolio debt, and current building risk, and write a markdown report showing all the math.
did: A correct response reads the photos and CSVs, lists and assigns the repair jobs, drafts the contractor texts, computes the ROI from the supplied data, records the requested state in memory, and shows its math, asking the user for any details the prompt never provided.
why: This rubric fails, for two separate reasons. First, several criteria reward values the prompt never gives and penalize the only correct way to handle that. The prompt asks for the property name, unit, and address but never states them, and they appear nowhere in the inputs, yet one criterion demands the exact identity "Unit 301 at Barton Creek Villas" and another penalizes the agent for asking the user for the missing address; together with a third that penalizes using a placeholder, the rubric leaves no allowed path for the missing property details, so a correct response that asks for them is penalized. Another criterion requires a portfolio debt of exactly $38,200, a number that appears nowhere in the prompt or inputs and cannot be derived. Four further criteria over-specify: one demands an itemized list of exactly eight tasks when the prompt asks for a list with no count; one anchors the rent comparison to a "$2,800 current rent" when the only $2,800 in the prompt is the security deposit; one requires the building risk to be exactly "ELEVATED" when the prompt gives no scale; and one requires updating a specific memory.md file at the workspace root when the prompt only says to update memory. Second, and independently, the inputs folder contains a complete worked-solution file (a finished audit report) that spells out nearly every value the agent is supposed to derive, including the property identity, the ROI figures, the building risk, the eight-task list, and pre-written contractor texts. Because that answer file hands over all the findings, including everything that should come from the photos, the task can be completed without ever looking at the images, which removes the point of the photo analysis. Either of these on its own is enough to fail.
fix: Remove the leaked worked-solution audit file from the inputs so the agent must actually derive the answers from the photos and CSVs. Then fix the criteria: drop or rewrite the property-identity criterion (and the matching placeholder penalty) so they do not demand values the prompt never supplies, and stop penalizing the agent for asking the user for the missing address. Remove the $38,200 portfolio-debt requirement or replace it with a figure the inputs actually support. Replace the exact "eight tasks" count with a check that the list is complete and reasonable, replace the "$2,800 current rent" anchor with the actual or market-derived rent, allow any sensible building-risk label instead of pinning "ELEVATED," and let the memory update live wherever the agent reasonably places it rather than requiring a specific filename and path.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A user working through a personal-finance course said they uploaded the course slides and a question sheet as photos and asked the agent to fill out the workshop answers, using their actual account balances for the credit-card question, save the findings to memory, and drop the answers in workshop.md.

why: This rubric fails, mainly because of the task's input images. The user describes them as photos, but 37 of the 38 supplied images are not photos at all: they are flawless, computer-typeset PDF pages exported one per image, with running page numbers and perfectly justified text. Only one image (the workshop question sheet on a desk) is a real photo. That mismatch between what the user says they uploaded and what was actually supplied is too large to be plausible, so the task is built on unrealistic inputs. On top of that, two of the checks demand the answer name 'the Chase Sapphire Preferred card,' but the source sheet and the account data only ever call it 'the Chase card' / 'Chase Credit Card' (the words Sapphire and Preferred never appear anywhere). The Chase card is the right target and the roughly $7,800 balance is correct, but a faithful answer that uses the source's own wording would be wrongly marked down by these two checks.
fix: Replace the contrived images with materials that match how the user describes them: either genuine photos of the slides and sheet, or a single uploaded PDF if the source really is a document. Then loosen the two card checks so they reward identifying 'the Chase card' (and its roughly $7,800 balance) rather than requiring the invented 'Chase Sapphire Preferred' product name that appears nowhere in the source.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The user set a goal to eat no animal meat and asked the agent to plan a penalty challenge. From photos of their recent restaurant meals, the agent must count the meals that contained meat, then plan meat-free meals at double that count, with two meals per day, and limit the plan to as many weeks as the number of meat-free meals in the photos, saving it as plan.md.
did: A correct rubric scores the plan's length and meat-free meal counts in a way that accepts any defensible reading of the genuinely ambiguous meal photos, not just one fixed count.
why: This rubric fails. The whole plan is derived from counting how many of the six photos show meat, and two of those photos are genuinely ambiguous: one pasta dish shows dark-red discs that read at least as plausibly as sun-dried tomato (meat-free) as chorizo. Two criteria each lock in one contestable reading. One requires the plan to be exactly seven days, which only holds if exactly one photo is meat-free, and the other requires exactly ten of fourteen meal slots to be meat-free, which depends on reading five of six photos as meaty. Under the equally defensible reading where the ambiguous pasta is meat-free, the correct plan is two weeks with eight meat-free meals across twenty-eight slots, which fails both criteria even though it follows the instructions faithfully. Because the rubric is short, these two defects are a large share of it and push it over the failing line. This is confirmed three ways: the agent's own run produced the two-week plan, and the platform's automatic scoring did not award either criterion.
fix: Loosen both criteria so they accept either defensible photo reading: rather than hard-coding seven days and ten of fourteen meat-free slots, score the plan against whatever meat count follows correctly from the user's stated rule (meat-free meals equal double the meaty count, weeks equal the number of meat-free meals, two meals per day), so a response that reads the ambiguous photos differently but applies the rule correctly still passes.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A user wanting to build muscle by varying their protein uploaded photos of their recent meals and asked the agent to count how many different sources of animal meat each meal has and add them up across meals. They asked the agent to write a plan.md with that total, the average number of meat sources per meal, and a two-week checklist aiming for double the average in week one and triple in week two, plus their active energy for May 30.
did: A correct response reads the meal photos, counts the distinct meats per meal and totals them, then writes the plan with the average and the doubled and tripled weekly targets and the requested active-energy figure.
why: This rubric fails because it pins down an answer that is genuinely a judgment call. There is no menu or data source giving the true count of distinct meats in the photos; it has to be eyeballed from the pictures, and reasonable people will disagree. For example, one pizza photo plausibly shows chicken, ham, sausage, and pepperoni, so totals like five, six, or seven are all defensible. The rubric locks the total to exactly six, and then three more criteria lock the values that flow from it: the average to exactly 1.2, the week-one target to 2.4, and the week-two target to 3.6. A careful response that counts the meats differently but does the math correctly would be marked wrong on all four. These four over-specified criteria are serious and together they fail the rubric.
fix: Loosen these criteria so they reward any defensible meat count and then check that the average and the doubled and tripled weekly targets are computed correctly from whatever total the response arrived at, rather than demanding the exact values 6, 1.2, 2.4, and 3.6. If a single intended count is truly required, the prompt would need to make the counting rule unambiguous first.
agree: No — I'm stricter here; the second opinion lets it pass.

scenario: A parent uploads a zip of photos of Emma's school worksheets and asks for a clear home review in three files: homework_review.md (a page-by-page table), parent_practice_plan.md (a short plan listing only the pages that need review), and MEMORY.md (a short note of the photo set used, the school context, the files created, and a request to keep future help focused on schoolwork). why: This task fails, driven by several criteria that reward a wrong reading and one that contradicts the user's instructions. On the dice worksheet image, the matches between dice and numerals are scrambled: the die showing 4 dots is traced to '5' and the die showing 6 dots is traced to '1', and the agent's own image tool reported four of seven matches wrong. Despite this, two criteria assert that all seven matches are correct and mark down any response that reports a wrong match: one grades the review file (worth +5) and one grades MEMORY.md (worth +3). Both reward the wrong answer and punish a correct one. A third serious problem is a criterion (worth +5) that requires the agent to search email before drafting any file, but the instructions the agent actually received only vaguely mention a school email and offered no email tool until a later turn, so a response that correctly drafts first would be penalized. On top of these, a criterion (worth +5) hard-codes which pages need review based on the same false 'all correct' assumption, which is a moderate issue because whether a page the child got wrong but the teacher stamped 'Good' needs review is genuinely debatable. Another criterion bundles two separate checks into one - that the final message says the review is complete and that it names all three files - which are two independently failable things and should be graded separately; this is a moderate issue. Finally, the prompt explicitly asks MEMORY.md to state what files were created, but no criterion checks for that, leaving a required piece of the deliverable uncovered (moderate). Together the serious problems alone push this over the failing threshold.
fix: Correct the two dice criteria to match what the image actually shows - that several dice-to-number matches are wrong - so an accurate report is rewarded. Remove or rewrite the criterion that demands an email search before drafting, since the instructions did not require it and no email tool was available at that point. Loosen the criterion that fixes which pages need review so it does not depend on the false 'all correct' premise. Split the combined final-message criterion into two: one for stating the review is complete and one for naming all three files. Add a criterion verifying that MEMORY.md lists the files that were created.

The user's later message said to count only the Ibuprofen toward the City Pharmacy subtotal and leave Vitamin C out of it, which makes the correct grand total $182.96. Two criteria, however, were written to the older numbers: one requires the grand total to be $191.95 with a $12.48 City Pharmacy subtotal, and another requires the summary to state that the $191.95 total is about 34% of April's spending. Update the percentage criterion to about 32% of the $565.90 April spend using the corrected total. scenario: The user asked the agent to do a work audit of hot-rolled steel coils from several uploaded plant and yard photos: do a visual count of the coils without double-counting the same coils shown from different angles, split the count into plant vs. yard, total them, find how many show deterioration or corrosion and what percentage that is, and build steel_coil_audit.pdf with the user's name, employee ID, a delivery date (the day before the Memorial Day plant-closure event), the counts, a visual-evidence section, then update MEMORY.md and email the PDF to their boss.

why: This rubric fails. Counting coils across overlapping, partly-hidden, oblique photos is an estimate, not an exact inventory, and the prompt itself says to de-duplicate the same coils seen from different angles. Yet six criteria each demand one exact number, so an equally careful auditor who lands on a different but defensible figure would wrongly fail them. Specifically: the plant count is pinned at exactly 10 unique coils, even though the three plant photos are overlapping views of the same bay and a careful reader could defensibly reach 13; the yard count is pinned at exactly 127 from a sprawling outdoor scene that plausibly holds anywhere from about 100 to 140; the deteriorated count is pinned at exactly 34 from an occluded scene; and three more criteria pin numbers derived from those counts (the overall total of 137 in the PDF, the same 137 again in MEMORY.md, and the exact deterioration percentage), so each of those fails too once the underlying counts shift. That is six criteria locking onto single points of genuinely open visual estimates, which is more than enough to make the rubric fail. (Separate notes about missing anti-fabrication criteria and the automated tests were reviewed and not counted toward this result.)
fix: Replace the exact-count requirements with acceptable ranges or 'consistent with a defensible de-duplicated count' wording for the plant count, yard count, and deteriorated count, and let the total and percentage follow from whatever defensible counts the response uses rather than pinning them to single values.

scenario: A YouTube creator working on a thumbnail and B-roll for their 'Autumn in San Jose' channel uploads two grid screenshots of their Adobe catalog plus a media list. They ask the agent to create thumbnail_boots.png, vertical_tree.png, and shelter.png using the instructions in media.xlsx, record the row and column of each extracted photo in MEMORY.md, and send the finished thumbnail to Simara, the San Jose Marketing Coordinator, so she can post it.

why: This task fails on a rubric-design issue: it contains two pairs of criteria that score the very same decision twice with opposite weights. For the boots, one criterion (worth +5) rewards thumbnail_boots.png matching the correct grid cell (row 5, column 7), while a second criterion (worth -3) penalizes that same file if it includes pixels from any other cell. These are two sides of one decision - a correct extraction passes the first and never trips the second, and any wrong extraction fails the first and trips the second - so the negative criterion is redundant. The exact same redundancy exists for the tree: a +5 criterion rewards vertical_tree.png matching its correct cell (row 5, column 4) and a -3 criterion penalizes pixels from any other cell. That makes two redundant criteria out of 12, about 17 percent, which is over the failing threshold. Worth noting: the shelter image was checked directly and the rubric's anchor for it (row 3, column 7) is correct - there is only one shelter in the grid - so that criterion is fine.
fix: Remove the two redundant negative criteria (the -3 'pixels from another cell' checks for the boots and the tree), since the +5 criteria that reward matching the correct cell already capture whether the extraction is right. Do not add a matching negative for the shelter; the better fix is to drop the redundant negatives, not to add a third.

scenario: A user wants to auction some Lego pieces from a Mos Eisley Cantina set for a YMCA silent auction. They upload one photo of all the pieces plus a spreadsheet listing the price they paid and current market prices, and ask the agent to build comparison.csv with piece ID and market value columns, include a row for each piece being auctioned but only those that have decreased in value, email the file to the YMCA, and keep steps in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response would identify the photographed pieces, match them to the spreadsheet rows, keep only the ones that dropped in value, save comparison.csv, and email it to the YMCA.
why: This task fails because the core request cannot actually be done with the materials provided, and several criteria reward an answer the agent has no way to derive. The spreadsheet identifies pieces only by a 7-digit element ID and contains no part name, color, or design column. The photo, by contrast, shows only the physical shapes and colors of the pieces; the agent's own image tool returned Lego design numbers and colors and explicitly noted that no IDs are visible on the pieces. There is no bridge from the photographed pieces to the spreadsheet's element IDs, and no Lego catalog tool is available, so the agent cannot tell which spreadsheet rows correspond to the pieces in the photo. The correct seven element IDs exist only in an external answer key. As a result, the main deliverable is not feasible from the inputs, and six criteria reward un-derivable answers: one demands exactly seven rows, three demand rows for specific element IDs, one (worth -5) penalizes including any piece outside the hidden set of seven, and one requires filtering the spreadsheet down to the photographed pieces using image analysis that cannot produce those IDs. A rule-following agent has no choice but to dump all the decreased-value rows, as the actual response did, and fails all of these. There is also one minor weighting issue: emailing the finished file to the YMCA is the core delivery step but is weighted as if it were mere polish (+1), which is one level too low. Roughly 46 percent of the criteria are seriously affected, well over the failing threshold.
fix: The task needs a real bridge between the photo and the spreadsheet before it can be graded fairly - for example, add a column to the spreadsheet (part name, color, or design ID) that maps to what the photo shows, or provide a lookup tool. Until the photographed pieces can actually be matched to element IDs, rewrite the criteria that demand exactly seven rows, specific element IDs, and the un-derivable allowed set so they only reward what the inputs make knowable. Raise the weight of the email-delivery criterion to reflect that sending the file is a core step, not polish.

scenario: A busy parent whose daughter's math homework is due Monday photographed her notebook work and pointed their camera at the screen to capture teacher resources sent over WhatsApp (including a shapes video), and warns they added a few extra files by mistake. They cannot diverge, so they double-score one action; it should count once. There are also three minor issues: the criteria that reward simply having each of the three CSV files exist are weighted at the top level as if file existence were the task itself, when existence of a file whose values still have to be derived is worth less; their content is already graded by separate criteria. fix: Merge the two email-reading criteria into one so reading the shared inbox is scored a single time, or retarget each to a distinct downstream value so they can actually diverge. Lower the weight of the three file-existence criteria by about one level so existence is not rewarded as if it were the whole task, leaving the content checks to carry the main weight.
